title: The Poison Cloud of Kirti Nagar and the Birth of Absolute Industrial Liability
hook: Following a toxic gas leak in west Delhi, a Constitution Bench replaced nineteenth-century exceptions with absolute liability for hazardous industries.
laws: Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Section 304A, Section 336, Section 337, and Section 338)

facts.label: Court
facts.value: Supreme Court of India (Five-Judge Constitution Bench)

facts.label: Incident Date
facts.value: December 4 and December 6, 1985 (oleum gas leaks from a chemical plant in west Delhi)

facts.label: Human Toll
facts.value: One practicing advocate died and hundreds of residents and workers were hospitalized

facts.label: Doctrinal Shift
facts.value: Replaced traditional strict liability and its exceptions with non-delegable absolute liability

summary: While a public interest petition seeking the relocation of a hazardous chemical and fertilizer unit in west Delhi was pending before the Supreme Court, a storage tank structure collapsed on December 4, 1985, releasing a dense cloud of oleum gas across surrounding neighbourhoods. Hundreds of people were hospitalized and an advocate died after inhaling the toxic fumes, followed two days later by a second leak from a defective valve that triggered closure orders under Section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

Legal aid bodies and the local bar association intervened to claim compensation for the victims under Article 32, prompting a five-judge Constitution Bench to examine whether private industrial enterprises could be held directly accountable in writ proceedings. The bench noted that nineteenth-century common law rules on strict liability allowed industrial defendants to escape responsibility through exceptions such as acts of third parties or unforeseen natural events.

On December 20, 1986, the Constitution Bench established the doctrine of absolute liability, holding that any enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute, non-delegable duty to the community with zero exceptions if harm occurs. The court further ruled that compensation must be correlated to the magnitude and financial capacity of the enterprise to ensure effective deterrence.

timeline.text: A second leak from a defective valve prompts authorities to order the plant closed under Section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

timeline.title: Absolute Liability Doctrine Announced
timeline.text: A five-judge Constitution Bench establishes absolute industrial liability without exceptions and links damages to enterprise capacity.

judgment.outcome: Reference answered by the five-judge Constitution Bench; the court affirmed broad remedial powers under Article 32 and established absolute liability without exceptions for enterprises carrying on hazardous or inherently dangerous activities.
points: An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to ensure no harm results to anyone.
The nineteenth-century English rule of strict liability and its traditional exceptions do not apply to hazardous industrial enterprises in India.
Compensation awarded against a hazardous enterprise must be proportionate to its magnitude and capacity so that damages carry a genuine deterrent effect.
Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to forge new remedies and award compensation in appropriate cases involving grave violations of fundamental rights.

principles.name: Doctrine of Absolute Liability
principles.meaning: Any enterprise carrying on a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity for profit is strictly and unconditionally liable for all resulting harm, without any common-law exceptions.
principles.inThisCase: The court rejected defenses such as third-party sabotage or unforeseen mechanical failure, making industrial safety an absolute legal obligation.

principles.name: Deep Pocket Principle of Deterrence
principles.meaning: The measure of compensation for industrial harm should scale with the size and financial capacity of the enterprise.
principles.inThisCase: The bench held that larger corporations must pay higher damages so that compensation acts as a meaningful deterrent against safety shortcuts.

principles.name: Remedial Scope of Article 32
principles.meaning: Constitutional writ jurisdiction includes the power to craft innovative remedies, not merely issue traditional prerogative writs.
principles.inThisCase: The court affirmed that Article 32 allows awarding compensation where fundamental rights to life are threatened by mass industrial hazards.

takeaways: Hazardous industries in India operate under an absolute, non-delegable duty of safety with zero common-law exceptions.
Industrial compensation is tied to enterprise scale and capacity to deter negligence in dense urban areas.
The ruling reshaped Indian environmental jurisprudence and paved the way for modern pollution and public liability statutes.

lawNote: Because the gas leaks occurred in December 1985, the proceedings were governed by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, alongside Articles 21 and 32 of the Constitution.

social.script: What happened when a toxic oleum gas cloud drifted over west Delhi in December 1985? A collapsed storage structure at a chemical plant hospitalized hundreds of residents and killed an advocate, followed by a second leak two days later. Traditional nineteenth-century common law allowed hazardous industries to escape damages through exceptions like third-party sabotage or unforeseen accidents. On December 20, 1986, a five-judge Constitution Bench rejected those loopholes. The court created the doctrine of absolute liability, holding hazardous enterprises unconditionally responsible with zero exceptions, and tied compensation to corporate capacity for real deterrence. You be the judge. Full case notes are on the Courtroom Chronicles website.
